claims.text: Applying a PVD-deposited, nanometer-scale Al2O3 coating to boride-based components will significantly improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
The Al2O3 coating will impede diffusion of aluminum into the boride substrate.
Direct exposure of boride-based components to molten aluminum at 700–750°C causes interfacial degradation through aluminum diffusion into the boride layer.
Boride-containing surfaces are relevant to components used in aluminum-processing environments.
A dense, continuous, nanometer-scale Al2O3 coating can be deposited by PVD onto the existing boride surface.
The Al2O3 layer will be inert and thermally stable at 700–750°C in molten aluminum.
A continuous, dense Al2O3 interface will block aluminum atoms from entering the boride substrate.
Reducing aluminum penetration will inhibit interfacial chemical interactions and thereby slow or prevent interfacial degradation and corrosion.
Sputter-deposited protective films can improve corrosion resistance.
Coated components will have less corrosion depth than untreated boride components under the specified molten-aluminum exposure.
Coated components will have lower interfacial aluminum diffusion than untreated boride components.
Coated components will lose less weight than untreated boride components.
Untreated boride-based components undergo significant interfacial corrosion and measurable degradation in high-temperature molten aluminum.
The coating's benefit should persist during prolonged hot-dip plating cycles at 700–750°C.
Coating thickness, deposition uniformity, adhesion, thermal stress, and extreme thermal cycling may affect coating performance.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction at p < 0.05 in the measured corrosion outcomes, or coating delamination, would falsify the hypothesis.
